You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Reducing weight to save energy and enhancing mechanical properties to increase safety level are both vital for structural materials in modern engineering. The lightweight steels have been promising for addressing these needs. However, the significant loss of ductility and strength in lightweight steels by localized accumulation of dislocations when strengthened by nanoprecipitates is a crucial problem. Here, we show an approach to overcome this dilemma by significant atomic-scale strain waves with extremely small wavelengths (<1 nm) and high amplitudes (up to 3%) in Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight steels. Such atomic-scale strain waves render the dislocation lines wavy and paired, which tangle into dense hexagonal dislocation networks via cross-slip at medium and late deformation stages, significantly enhancing defect-storage capacity and strain hardening ability. The atomic-scale strain waves also promote the dynamic refinement of slip bands upon deformation. These mechanisms are active in both steel variants with and without nanoscale coherent κ-carbides, enabling unprecedentedly strong and ductile lightweight steels. The strategy of tuning atomic-scale strain waves thus provides an important avenue for designing stronger and more ductile lightweight materials for key structural engineering.

---

## Introduction

The reduction of weight while maintaining or even enhancing strength and ductility of metallic materials is a burning task for saving energy, reducing carbon dioxide emissions and ensuring sustainable reliability for safety-critical parts in various industries1,2. The strength and ductility also act as decisive indexes for the measurement of many other mechanical properties including fatigue resistance3,4 and fracture toughness5. The lightweight Fe-Mn-Al-C steels with face-centered cubic (FCC) austenitic matrix are one of the most promising candidates for addressing the demand of low mass density at excellent strength-ductility synergy1,6-9. The mechanical properties of lightweight steels can be substantially contributed by the precipitation strengthening from different types of nanoprecipitates, e.g., coherent L1 -(Fe, Mn) AlC κ-carbide with ordered FCC structure, and incoherent NiAl B2 phase with ordered body-centered cubic (BCC) structure8-10. However, the shearing of the κ-carbide during plastic deformation at higher stress leads to the local softening, which can cause localized dislocation accumulation and significantly deteriorate the ductility of austenitic lightweight steels6,11,12. Moreover, the κ-carbides at grain boundaries are incoherent with austenitic matrix, which promotes crack initiation and propagation, leading to embrittlement13,14. The B2 (ordered BCC) particles are usually hard to be sheared and hence dislocations need to bypass them9, which leaves additional dislocation loops around the particles behind, leading to remarkable strengthening effect. However, this is usually accompanied with a significant expense of ductility due to dislocation pile-up and stress localization at the intrinsically brittle B2 intermetallic phase13,15.

Recently, a dual-nanoprecipitation approach has been proposed to further enhance the mechanical properties of lightweight steels by simultaneously triggering both nanosized shearable κ-carbides and non-shearable B2 particles1. However, the Orowan looping mechanism in this dual-nanoprecipitation system still increases the stress concentrations and leads to a substantial reduction in ductility13. Another shearable α-phase (disordered BCC) from γ decomposition (γ→ γ+α) has also been introduced into lightweight steels to enhance the mechanical properties16,17.

Such duplex lightweight steels can exhibit multi-stage strain hardening characteristics with sequential activation of deformation mechanisms in the α-phase and γ-matrix18. However, the different deformability of the α- and γ-phases leads to decohesion with stress concentrations at their interphases, which are susceptible to crack nucleation and can cause a substantial reduction in damage tolerance19.

Linear lattice defects carry the plasticity in the lightweight steels. However, their accumulations cause stress concentrations, acting as the fundamental mechanism in restricting the enhancement of mechanical properties. To overcome this dilemma, in this work we propose a strategy to tune the atomic-scale strain waves to alleviate the micro- and nano-scale stress concentrations in lightweight steels, which is validated by the significantly enhanced strength-ductility synergy. This concept is demonstrated in a prototype lightweight steel with nominal composition Fe Mn Al C (at.%) designed through thermodynamic calculations using FactSage software with the FSstel steel database (Supplementary Figure 1). Guided by the calculated phase diagrams, thermomechanical processing steps (e.g., hot-rolling, homogenization, cold-rolling, annealing and aging) with proper parameters were performed to tailor the subnanoscale κ'-carbides (present as local chemical orders) which enable the tuning of atomic-scale wave-like strain distribution. Accordingly, the otherwise damage-prone stress concentrations can be relieved by the well-tuned atomic-scale strain waves. This approach can also boost planar slip, further promoting the strain hardening ability in the loading stages. The present study thus suggests a promising path toward the development of strong and ductile lightweight steels for advanced structural engineering applications.

---

## Results

The present lightweight steel in homogenized condition is characterized by a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC-γ) austenitic structure, showing homogeneous elemental distribution at the micro-scale without any grain boundary (GB) precipitates (Supplementary Figure 2). The stacking fault energy (SFE) of the steel is relatively high, i.e., ~82 mJ/m2 according to the weak-beam dark-field (DF) STEM characterization (Supplementary Figure 3) and ~78 mJ/m2 calculated by the subregular solution model6,20 (see Supplementary Information). The atomic-scale strain wave in the material was tuned via adjusting the time periods of annealing after cold-rolling. The samples annealed at 900 oC for short time (3 min) and that for longer time (30 min) are denoted as SA and LA, respectively. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Supplementary Figure 4) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) phase maps (Fig. 1a, b) reveal the FCC structure in both LA and SA bulk steels. As shown in Fig. 1a-b, abundant annealing twin boundaries (TBs) are present in both steels. The average grain sizes excluding annealing TBs in steels LA and SA are 15.0 ± 9.7 μm and 7.5 ± 5.4 μm, respectively, according to EBSD analysis from multiple areas in each sample. The bright-field (BF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images (Supplementary Figure 5a, c) and corresponding energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mappings (Supplementary Figure 5b, d) suggest that the steels LA and SA show homogeneous elemental distribution at the micro- and nano-scales. In the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns (inserts in Fig. 1c, d) taken along the zone axis of [001] , the inherently faint γ diffraction spots from specific {100} superlattice diffraction signal of κ'-carbide are visible in both steels LA and SA. More specifically, dark-field (DF) imaging was used to visualize the κ'-carbide domains and the results are shown in Fig. 1c, d, which indicates that the average sizes of κ'-carbide are 0.4 nm and 0.5 nm with average area fractions of 8.5% and 16.5% in steels LA and SA, respectively. The abnormal decreases of fraction and size of the sub-nanoscale κ'-carbides with increasing annealing time from 3 min to 30 min is related to the formation kinetics of κ'-carbide. Specifically, the high atomic mobility promoted by crystalline defects induced in the prior deformation strongly facilitates the formation kinetics of sub-nanoscale κ'-carbides during annealing at the first few minutes, leading to the deviation of associated crystal lattice from thermodynamic equilibrium. However, upon further increasing annealing time, the prolonged exposure of the fully recrystallized microstructure at 900 oC can lead to the partial dissolution of the previously formed sub-nanoscale κ'-carbide, rendering the crystal lattice closer to the thermodynamic equilibrium state.

Atomic-resolution high-angle angular dark field (HAADF) STEM technique was performed in the exploration of the κ'-carbide domains in steels LA and SA. The atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images overlapped with the inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) maps in Fig. 1e, f outline the distribution of κ'-carbide domains in the FCC lattices of the two steels, whereas the contrasts of the different atomic columns indicates that the elements are nonuniformly distributed at the atomic-scale. The atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM image of steel LA acquired along [011] γ zone axis in Supplementary Figure 6a and the EDS analysis result in Supplementary Figure 6b, c suggest that Al tends to be enriched in specific atomic columns. The atomic-scale distributions of Fe and Mn are also inhomogeneous, but are more uniform compared to that of Al. Specifically, Fe-rich columns are Mn-depleted, and the two types of atomic columns are adjacent to each other. This may arise from the zero mixing enthalpy between Fe and Mn, and thus they neither attract nor repel each other21,22. The negative mixing enthalpies of Fe-Al (-11 KJ/mol) and Mn-Al (-19 KJ/mol)23 provide the thermodynamic driving force for the formation of κ'-carbide. In the κ'-carbide domains, the average atomic fractions of Fe, Mn and Al for atomic columns on the (11̅1) plane show wave-like fluctuations with wavelength doubling the spacing of the crystal plane (Supplementary Figure 6d).

Atom probe tomography (APT) was also performed to analyze chemical features of the κ'-carbides. The 3D reconstruction maps of typical cubes in Supplementary Figure 7e, f show the clustering behavior in steels LA and SA, respectively. The calculated radial distribution functions (RDFs) of Fe and Mn around Al atoms (Supplementary Figure 7g) show bulk-normalized Al-(Fe/Mn) concentration ratios exceeding unity at the subnanoscale. Notably, these ratios are higher in steel SA than that in steel LA, indicating that more Al-(Fe/Mn) bonds contribute to the formation of κ'-carbide domains in steel SA. This is consistent with the statistical results for the fractions of κ'-carbides from the DF-TEM images in Fig. 1c, d. The average Al concentration within the κ'-carbides is ~18.1 at. % and ~22.3 at. % for steels LA and SA, respectively. Since the atomic radius of Al (0.143 nm) is remarkably larger than Fe/Mn (0.124 nm), significant lattice expansion and contraction can occur at the Al-rich κ'-carbide domains and Al-depleted FCC-γ matrix, respectively, which can further induce atomic-scale strain fluctuations in the steels.

The atomic-scale strain fluctuation was further explored by the geometric phase analysis (GPA) method25,26 based on HAADF-STEM images, e.g., shown in Fig. 1g, h. The ε strain maps xx show the atomic-scale tension-compression strain distributions in steels LA and SA with statistical average strain values (total pixels) of 0.26% nm-2 and 1.06% nm-2, respectively (Fig. 1g, h). This indicates that steel LA undergoes greater lattice expansion than steel SA. Further, the results suggest that the atomic-scale strain waves are primarily derived from the lattice expansion and contraction at the sub-nano-sized Al-rich κ'-carbide domains and Al-depleted FCC-γ matrix, respectively, resulting in a fluctuating tension-compression strain distribution at atomic scale. Fig. 1i shows the line profiles of atomic-scale strains along the [200] γ direction, revealing the wave-like distribution with crests and valleys. The average wavelength of atomic-scale strains along the [200] γ direction in steel SA (0.84 ± 0.27 nm) is smaller than that in steel LA (0.98 ± 0.38 nm), while the average amplitude in steel SA (1.71 ± 0.70%) is higher than that in steel LA (0.82 ± 0.32%). The ε strain maps in Supplementary Figure 8 also shows the higher strain amplitude and smaller wavelength of the atomic-scale strains in steel SA than those in steel LA. This can be attributed to the higher Al concentration and larger fraction of κ'-carbides in steel SA, as discussed above.

Further, the original steels LA and SA were aged at 600 oC for 40 min to trigger the formation of nanosized L1 -(Fe, Mn) AlC (x<1) κ-carbide, and the resultant materials are denoted by LA-A and SA-A, respectively. XRD patterns (Supplementary Figure 4) and EBSD phase maps (Supplementary Figure 9a, e) confirm the FCC structure in both LA-A and SA-A bulk steels. The average grain sizes excluding annealing TBs in steels LA-A and SA-A are equal to steels LA and SA, respectively, according to EBSD analysis from multiple areas in each sample. This confirms that the aging treatment did not change the grain sizes in the steels. The EDS mappings (Supplementary Figure 9d, h) for the areas captured by BF-STEM images (Supplementary Figure 9c, g) suggest homogeneous elemental distribution at the micro-scale in both steels. However, in the SAED patterns in Fig. 2a, b taken along the zone axis of [001] γ, the {100} superlattice diffraction spots of κ'- and κ-carbides with ordered structures are distinctly visible in both steels LA and SA. This is consistent to the previous finding that the κ'-carbide can serve as a precursor for the formation of κ-carbide by further ordering of C into the body-centered octahedral interstitial positions via spinodal decomposition 6,7. The DF images stemming from the diffraction spot of (110) κ'/κ in Fig. 2c, d light up the κ- and κ'-carbide domains. The average sizes of κ-carbide in steels LA-A and SA-A are 6.1 ± 1.7 nm and 6.0 ± 1.2 nm, respectively. The HAADF-STEM images in Fig. 2e and f reveal the atomic-scale structures of κ-carbides in steels LA-A and SA-A, respectively. The ε xx strain maps in Fig. 2g, h by GPA method using the vectors of (200) γ and (020) γ also show the wave-like tension-compression strain fluctuations in atomic scale. The statistical strain values (total pixels) are 16.87% nm-2 and 6.5% nm-2 in steels LA-A and SA-A, respectively. Fig. 2i shows the line profiles of atomic-scale strains along the [020] γ direction. The matrixes containing sub-nano-sized κ'-carbide domains show atomic-scale strain waves with the average amplitude of 1.84 ± 0.89% and 1.01 ± 0.48% in steels SA-A and LA-A, respectively, similar to those in the as-annealed steels without aging (SA and LA). Moreover, the interiors of aging-induced nano-sized κ-carbide phase regions in steels SA-A and LA-A also exhibit wave-like periodic fluctuations with the average amplitude of 1.59 ± 0.42% and 1.16 ± 0.58%, respectively. For the steel LA-A, the atomic-scale strain waves in the κ-carbide phase are almost tension with average value of wave peaks and troughs to be about 1.58%, which is higher than that in the matrix (~0.06%), suggesting that the atomic-scale strain distributions in the κ-carbide and matrix are distinctly different. However, in the steel SA-A, the atomic-scale strain distributions in the κ-carbide and matrix are fairly similar as indicated by the small differences in average amplitudes (1.59% and 1.84%, respectively) and average strain values (0.09% and -0.24%, respectively).

Fig. 3a shows the tensile engineering stress-strain curves of the steels at room temperature. The steel SA characterized by atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength exhibits a yield strength value (𝜎 y) of 687 ± 13 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (𝜎 u) of 1154 ± 4 MPa and a total elongation (𝜀 f) of 67.8% ± 4.0%, which are significantly higher than those values of steel LA (610 ± 10 MPa, 1035 ± 9 MPa and 37.8% ± 2.3%, respectively) with atomic-scale strain waves of lower amplitude and larger wavelength. The enhancements in strength and ductility achieved by tuning atomic-scale strain waves can also be observed when comparing the steels SA-A and LA-A with κ-carbide precipitation strengthening effect. More specific, the steel SA-A has a yield strength (𝜎 y) of 1073 ± 10 MPa and an ultimate tensile strength (𝜎 u) of 1325 ± 8 MPa at a total elongation (𝜀 f) of 50.4% ± 3.2%, which are superior than those of steel LA-A (1051 ± 8 MPa, 1242 ± 13 MPa and 20.1% ± 1.3%, respectively). The steels SA and SA-A exhibit not only enhanced strength and ductility but also superior work-hardening abilities compared to steels LA and LA-A, respectively (Fig. 3b). This is correlated with the modulated dislocation behaviors via tuning atomic-scale strain waves, as specifically discussed next. The above results suggest that the current strategy of tuning atomic-scale strain waves can allow for overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off that are presented in previous steels. Moreover, this strategy can be combined with the coherent nanoprecipitation approach to jointly enhance the strength-ductility combination, as can be confirmed by comparing the tensile curves of the present aged steels containing nano-sized κ-carbides (SA-A, LA-A) and that of the as-annealed variants free of nano-sized κ-carbides (SA, LA).

To avoid sample size effect, the uniform elongation values were used in the comparison of strength-ductility combinations shown in Fig. 3c (see details in Supplementary Table 3). Evidently, the strength-ductility combinations of the present lightweight steels SA and SA-A surpass that of previous lightweight steels, including those with κ-carbide precipitation strengthening 11,12,17,27,28, κ-carbide plus B2 particles strengthening 1,9,13,15,29, and duplex structure composed of FCC-γ and BCC-α phases with κ-carbide precipitation strengthening 18,19,30,31. Further, the products of specific ultimate tensile strength (SUTS) and uniform elongation (UE) of the steels SA and SA-A reach 8.5 and 7.4 GPa·g-1·cm3·%, respectively, which are unprecedentedly high compared to those obtained in previous studies, as shown in Fig. 3d. We also converted the total elongation values from references and our work into those corresponding to identical standard specimen dimensions by the Barba’s law, and accordingly the converted total elongation (CTE) is used in the additional comparison (see the calculation details in Supplementary Information) 32-34. As presented in Supplementary Figure 11, the products of SUTS and CTE of the present lightweight steels SA and SA-A surpass that of the previous lightweight steels.

The atomic-scale strain waves can also modulate the lattice constants of the present lightweight steels (Supplementary Table 2) and thus affect the elastic moduli. As displayed in Supplementary Table 4, the elastic moduli of steels SA and SA-A are higher than those of steels LA and LA-A, respectively. Further, shear modulus associated with the elastic modulus is of significance for determining the Peierls-Nabarro (P-N) stress that required to make a dislocation glide in a crystal without the assistance of thermal activation. Accordingly, the yield strength values for steels SA and LA ascribed from the significant lattice friction are estimated to be ~590 MPa and ~581 MPa, respectively (see the calculation details in Supplementary Information). Grain boundary strengthening also act as an effective mechanism that contribute to the yield strength of the steels, and the corresponding values for steels SA (average grain size of ~7.5 μm) and LA (average grain size of ~15.0 μm) are ~208 MPa and ~147 MPa, respectively (see Supplementary Information). In addition, the κ-carbide can provide significant precipitation strengthening as can be demonstrated by the observation that the yield strength values of steels LA-A and SA-A are higher than steels LA and SA, respectively. Further calculations suggest that the precipitation strengthening contributions from the κ-carbide for steels LA-A and SA-A are ~468 MPa and ~460 MPa, respectively (see Supplementary Information).

To elucidate the underlying deformation mechanisms responsible for the enhanced mechanical properties of the present steels, the deformed microstructures in the tensile-tested samples were characterized and compared at the identical deformation stages with various local strain levels at micro-, nano- and atomic scales. At the medium uniform deformation stages of steels LA and LA-A (i.e., local strains of ~20% and ~10%, respectively), the microstructures are characterized by a series of discrete planar slip bands along {111} γ planes with statistical average spacing of 411.6 ± 168.6 nm and 94.2 ± 86.3 nm, respectively, as shown in Fig. 4a and b. The intense dislocations that progressively tangled into high-density dislocation walls (HDDWs) along intersecting {111} γ slip planes are also observed. With increasing local strain to ~45% for steel LA at the late uniform deformation stage, the deformation microstructures are characterized by the progressive refinement of slip bands with a statistical average spacing reduction to 54.8 ± 35.8 nm (Fig. 4c). For steel LA-A, when local strain increases to ~15% (late uniform deformation stage), it maintains comparable slip band spacing of 93.4 ± 79.2 nm relative to prior strain levels (Fig. 4d). During the necking stages, upon further increasing local strain to ~70% and ~30% for steels LA and LA-A, the average spacings of slip bands are 54.4 ± 20.1 nm and 91.6 ± 58.3 nm, respectively (Supplementary Figure 12 and 13), suggesting that further slip band refinement in both steels is insignificant. Also, the distribution of slip bands is relatively heterogeneous, particularly in steel LA-A (Supplementary Figures 12 and 13).

The deformation microstructures of steels SA and SA-A are shown in Fig. 4e-h. At local strains of ~15% and ~10% (early uniform deformation stages) for steels SA and SA-A, respectively, the paired dislocations are regularly arranged within the matrix (Fig. 4e, f). The planar slip bands are also observed along {111} γ planes in the steel SA as displayed in Fig. 4e, with a statistical average spacing of 121.7 ± 49.7 nm. The increase of local strains to ~50% and ~30% at late uniform deformation stages for steels SA and SA-A, respectively, leads to the significant multiplication of planar slip bands and the increase in the number density of dislocations within individual bands, as displayed in Fig. 4g, h. At these strain levels, the statistical average spacings of slip bands in steels SA and SA-A are 39.3 ± 14.0 nm and 76.8 ± 47.5 nm, respectively. The nanoscale well-organized hexagonal dislocation networks on {111} γ planes are observed in both steels SA and SA-A. Further increasing local strains to ~75% and ~50% for steels SA and SA-A during necking stages leads to the reducing of slip band spacings to 34.3 ± 14.1 nm and 48.8 ± 30.7 nm, respectively (Supplementary Figures 12 and 13).

According to the above results, the morphologies of dislocations in plastically deformed steels SA and SA-A at early and medium uniform deformation stages are distinctly different. This is clearly illustrated by the amplified LAADF-STEM images in Supplementary Figure 14 which shows paired dislocations in steel SA and long dislocation lines in steel LA. This suggests that the atomic-scale strain waves in the steels significantly affect the slip of dislocations and thus their configuration. When the slip of leading dislocation is barriered by the strain wave peaks or troughs, the succeeding dislocation is likely to pile up and aggregate around the nearby region, which facilitates the formation of paired dislocations35. Also, in front of a dislocation line, the strain waves can induce the fluctuations of driving force levels. Thus, the dislocations slip by nanoscale segments that cut through the peaks or troughs of the strain waves. This results in a variant of stick-slip, and the moving dislocation lines become wavy as each segment responds differently. The conversion of an initially straight dislocation line into a wavy configuration also shortens the length to minimize the total energy of the dislocations. This rationalizes the shorter paired-dislocations in steel SA compared with the longer and smoother dislocation lines in steel LA (Supplementary Figure 14). The mechanisms for the formation of short and wavy paired dislocations can also be activated in steel SA-A. Thus, the atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength lead to the local pinning effect that makes overall dislocation movement sluggish, improving the strength levels of steels SA and SA-A.

In the present study, typical planar slip bands are observed in the deformed microstructures of the steels at various local strain levels, which are also commonly found in previous lightweight steels12,36,37. The inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) images in Fig. 4i, j shows the planar slip planes marked by red arrows and the edge dislocations with the Burgers vector of 𝑎/2 [01̅1] for steels LA and SA (with local strains of ~20% and ~15%, respectively). The formation of slip bands by dislocation planar slip is closely related to the stacking fault energy (SFE). The generalized SFE of the present lightweight steel estimated by thermodynamic calculation is ~78 mJ/m2 and the experimentally measured value is ~82 mJ/m2 (see Supplementary Information), which are comparably high. This SFE level would facilitate the planar slip in the steel during plastic deformation38. Notably, the local SFE can be variable from one site to another in the present lightweight steels due to the chemical fluctuation caused by the κ'-carbide. More specific, high Al concentration zones at κ'-carbide domains can be incorporated to push the magnitude of SFE up, while Fe/Mn-rich zones are particularly effective in reducing the local SFE39,40. The lower local SFE can widen the dissociate distance of two Shockley partial dislocations, which promotes the planar slip of dislocations on the initial slip plane. Thus, the atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength in steels SA and SA-A can bring in drastic fluctuations of local SFE and promote the planar slip of dislocations during plastic deformation. The planar slip of shorter paired dislocations in steels SA and SA-A bring finer slip bands than that in steels LA and LA-A (Supplementary Figure 13). Then the formation and refinement of planar slip bands during plastic deformation can provide significant dynamic Hall-Petch effect for enhancing strain-hardening ability over the deformation process, which significantly contributes to the high ductility at high strength levels41.

During plastic deformation, when the movement of dislocations is hindered on its primary slip plane, the increasing strain can promote a propensity for cross-slip of dislocations to accommodate plastic flow. The possibility of dislocation cross-slip strongly depends on the SFE. The relatively high SFE of the present steels can facilitate dislocation cross-slip by narrowing the dissociation width of perfect dislocations. This also helps to store dislocations and promotes their reactions in the steels. In the steels LA and LA-A, the cross-slip of long dislocation lines can facilitate the formation of HDDWs during plastic deformation, which can induce stress localization and is certainly adverse to the ductility42. Notably, the short paired dislocations in steels SA and SA-A can cross-slip and lead to the formation of dense hexagonal dislocation networks43. This corresponds to shorter dislocation lines and hence lower energy, which can significantly improve the tolerance for dislocation accumulation in the steels during plastic deformation. With the increased dislocation storage capacity, the dynamic formation of hexagonal dislocation networks significantly enhance the strain hardening ability and strength-ductility synergy.

In summary, we have developed unprecedentedly strong and ductile lightweight steel by inducing significant atomic-scale alternating tension-compression strain waves, which are formed by lattice expansion in Al-rich short-range ordered κ'-carbide domains and contraction in Fe/Mn-rich FCC-γ matrix. Upon mechanical loading, these atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength significantly increase the lattice friction, contributing to the high yield strength. During plastic deformation, the atomic-scale strain waves convert the straight dislocation lines into wavy and paired. The increase of engineering strains can force the paired dislocations tangle into dense hexagonal dislocation networks via cross-slip, which significantly enhances the defect-storage capacity of the steel. The atomic-scale strain waves can also promote the dynamic microstructure refinement with the reduction in the average spacing of planar slip bands during plastic deformation. These mechanisms jointly suppress localized stress concentrations and promote strain hardening ability, rendering the steels ultra-strong and ductile. The demonstrated strategy of tuning atomic-scale strain waves is thus promising for guiding the development of ultra-strong and ductile lightweight materials for advanced structural engineering applications.

---

## Methods

Thermodynamic calculations
The thermodynamic calculations by Factsage software 8.3 with the FSstel database were carried out to design the Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight steel. The phase diagrams illustrating the phase evolution with respect to the variations of C, Al and Mn contents and temperature are given in Supplementary Figure 1a-c, respectively. The C content of 5 at.% was selected to achieve a single FCC-γ phase above ~900 °C and κ-carbide precipitation below ~650 °C. To avoid the presence of BCC-α ferrite, the Al content of 15 at.% was chosen for the design. Additionally, a relatively high Mn content of 30 at.% was selected due to its role in stabilizing austenitic matrix and reducing the precipitation temperature of κ-carbide. As illustrated in Supplementary Figure 1d, the predicted phase configurations in the designed Fe Mn Al C lightweight steel indicate the high potential to achieve a microstructure consisting of austenite matrix and κ-carbide precipitates.

Material processing
A 5 kg Fe Mn Al C lightweight steel ingot, prepared using a commercial vacuum-induction furnace by melting pure Fe, Mn, Al and graphite (purity >99.9 wt.%), was ordered outside. The exact chemical compositions of the lightweight steel measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) and carbon-sulfur analyzer (CS744) are listed in Supplementary Table 1. A piece of lightweight steel with a thickness of 10 mm was cut from the ingot followed by hot rolling at 900 oC with a thickness reduction of 50%. Then the plate was homogenized at 1200 oC for 2 h followed by water quenching. Cold-rolling was conducted with a thickness reduction of 70%. Recrystallization annealing processes with short time (3 min) and longer time (30 min) were conducted at 900 oC followed by water quenching, and the annealed steel samples are denoted as LA and SA, respectively. Precipitation aging was performed at 600 oC for 40 min based on steels LA and SA, and the aged steel samples are denoted as LA-A and SA-A, respectively. During homogenization, annealing and aging, the lightweight steel samples were hermetically sealed in vacuum quartz tubes to avoid oxidation. The heat treatments were carried out in a box furnace and ended with water quenching in a water bath.

Mechanical characterization
Rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and a gauge width of 2.5 mm were machined inhouse by electrical discharge machining (DK 7720, China) according to the standard of ASTM E8 (different specimen sizes are allowed) 44. Room temperature uniaxial tensile tests were conducted by a Sansi 10 kN machine with an engineering strain rate of 1×10-3 s-1. The digital image correlation (DIC) method using the Aramis system (GOM GmbH) was used to precisely determine local strain evolution during tensile testing.

The product of specific ultimate tensile strength (SUTS) and tensile elongation (TE) was calculated as (UTS×TE)/𝜌, where 𝜌 is the mass density. The mass density of the present steel are estimated based on the regression formula45:
1/𝜌 = ∑ 𝐶𝑖/𝜌𝑖 (1)
where 𝜌𝑖 is the mass density of element i and 𝐶𝑖 is the mass fraction of element i.

The elastic modulus and nanohardness values were determined by nanoindentation at room temperature using a KLA G200X indentation tester with a Berkovich tip. During nanoindentation test, 16 indents were arranged in a square with the spacing between adjacent indents of 5 μm to avoid the overlap of plastic zones.

Microstructural characterization
The phase constituents of the steel samples were measured by X-ray diffraction (D/max-B 2550, Rigaku, Japan) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis with Hough transform was carried out using a Tescan Clara scanning electron microscope (SEM) with EDAX OIM data collection software at a voltage of 20.0 keV and 7.0 nA with a working distance of 15.0 mm and a step size of 100 nm. Back-scattered electron (BSE) imaging and electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) were performed at a voltage of 30.0 keV and 3.0 nA with a working distance of 10.0 mm. Energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) analysis based on the SEM was carried out with a working distance of 15.0 mm. The average grain sizes of the steels were determined based on EBSD measurements using TSL OIM 8.0 analysis software, with all data points above a threshold CI (Confidence Index) value of 0.1. The samples for SEM observations were prepared by grinding using silicon carbide paper from 400 to 5000 granulation and polishing using 3 μm diamond suspension and 20 nm silica dioxide suspension.

For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis, a ThermoFisher Talos F200X instrument was operated at a voltage of 200 kV. The probe convergence angle was 10.6 mrad for STEM imaging. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF), low-angle annular dark-field (LAADF) and bright field (BF) STEM images were obtained at collecting angles of 50-200 mrad, 30-50 mrad, and 0-30 mrad, respectively. The ThermoFisher Spectra 300 instrument was also used for atomic-resolution STEM observation operated at a voltage of 300 kV. The probe convergence angle and collecting angle for the atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images were 25.0 mrad and 50-200 mrad, respectively. To prepare samples for S/TEM analysis, disc specimens with a diameter of 3 mm were cut from the gauge region of tensile-tested samples at various local strain levels and non-deformation samples and ground to a thickness of ~50 μm followed by electron polishing using a twin-jet electron-polisher at a temperature of -30 °C. The electrolyte used for the electron polishing was a solution of 90% methanol and 10% perchloric acid. The atomic-scale strain maps were obtained by the geometric phase analysis (GPA) method based on the atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images using the strain++ 1.7.1 software. To ensure high reliability of the strain results, HAADF-STEM imaging was performed with drift correction by the piezo stage controller. The image was reconstructed after filtering out high-frequency noise to improve the signal‐to‐noise ratio, thereby enhancing the precision and accuracy of atomic-scale strain measurements 24.

For atom probe tomography (APT) analysis, the tips were prepared inhouse by a two-stage electro-polishing method. In the first stage, the samples with dimensions of 0.5×0.5×10 mm were polished using a 25 vol% perchloric/acetic acid solution at 15 V under the D.C. condition to prepare a rough needle. Then the needle samples were polished to a suitable sharpness using 2 vol% perchloric acid in 2-butoxyethanol solution at 5 V under the D.C. condition. APT analysis was carried out using CAMECA LEAP 5000 XR in voltage-pulsing mode with a repetition rate of 200 kHz and a pulse fraction of 15% at 50 K.

## Paper

## Abstract

Reducing weight to save energy and enhancing mechanical properties to increase safety level are both vital for structural materials in modern engineering. The lightweight steels have been promising for addressing these needs. However, the significant loss of ductility and strength in lightweight steels by localized accumulation of dislocations when strengthened by nanoprecipitates is a crucial problem. Here, we show an approach to overcome this dilemma by significant atomic-scale strain waves with extremely small wavelengths (<1 nm) and high amplitudes (up to 3%) in Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight steels. Such atomic-scale strain waves render the dislocation lines wavy and paired, which tangle into dense hexagonal dislocation networks via cross-slip at medium and late deformation stages, significantly enhancing defect-storage capacity and strain hardening ability. The atomic-scale strain waves also promote the dynamic refinement of slip bands upon deformation. These mechanisms are active in both steel variants with and without nanoscale coherent κ-carbides, enabling unprecedentedly strong and ductile lightweight steels. The strategy of tuning atomic-scale strain waves thus provides an important avenue for designing stronger and more ductile lightweight materials for key structural engineering.

---

## Introduction

The reduction of weight while maintaining or even enhancing strength and ductility of metallic materials is a burning task for saving energy, reducing carbon dioxide emissions and ensuring sustainable reliability for safety-critical parts in various industries1,2. The strength and ductility also act as decisive indexes for the measurement of many other mechanical properties including fatigue resistance3,4 and fracture toughness5. The lightweight Fe-Mn-Al-C steels with face-centered cubic (FCC) austenitic matrix are one of the most promising candidates for addressing the demand of low mass density at excellent strength-ductility synergy1,6-9. The mechanical properties of lightweight steels can be substantially contributed by the precipitation strengthening from different types of nanoprecipitates, e.g., coherent L1 -(Fe, Mn) AlC κ-carbide with ordered FCC structure, and incoherent NiAl B2 phase with ordered body-centered cubic (BCC) structure8-10. However, the shearing of the κ-carbide during plastic deformation at higher stress leads to the local softening, which can cause localized dislocation accumulation and significantly deteriorate the ductility of austenitic lightweight steels6,11,12. Moreover, the κ-carbides at grain boundaries are incoherent with austenitic matrix, which promotes crack initiation and propagation, leading to embrittlement13,14. The B2 (ordered BCC) particles are usually hard to be sheared and hence dislocations need to bypass them9, which leaves additional dislocation loops around the particles behind, leading to remarkable strengthening effect. However, this is usually accompanied with a significant expense of ductility due to dislocation pile-up and stress localization at the intrinsically brittle B2 intermetallic phase13,15.

Recently, a dual-nanoprecipitation approach has been proposed to further enhance the mechanical properties of lightweight steels by simultaneously triggering both nanosized shearable κ-carbides and non-shearable B2 particles1. However, the Orowan looping mechanism in this dual-nanoprecipitation system still increases the stress concentrations and leads to a substantial reduction in ductility13. Another shearable α-phase (disordered BCC) from γ decomposition (γ→ γ+α) has also been introduced into lightweight steels to enhance the mechanical properties16,17.

Such duplex lightweight steels can exhibit multi-stage strain hardening characteristics with sequential activation of deformation mechanisms in the α-phase and γ-matrix18. However, the different deformability of the α- and γ-phases leads to decohesion with stress concentrations at their interphases, which are susceptible to crack nucleation and can cause a substantial reduction in damage tolerance19.

Linear lattice defects carry the plasticity in the lightweight steels. However, their accumulations cause stress concentrations, acting as the fundamental mechanism in restricting the enhancement of mechanical properties. To overcome this dilemma, in this work we propose a strategy to tune the atomic-scale strain waves to alleviate the micro- and nano-scale stress concentrations in lightweight steels, which is validated by the significantly enhanced strength-ductility synergy. This concept is demonstrated in a prototype lightweight steel with nominal composition Fe Mn Al C (at.%) designed through thermodynamic calculations using FactSage software with the FSstel steel database (Supplementary Figure 1). Guided by the calculated phase diagrams, thermomechanical processing steps (e.g., hot-rolling, homogenization, cold-rolling, annealing and aging) with proper parameters were performed to tailor the subnanoscale κ'-carbides (present as local chemical orders) which enable the tuning of atomic-scale wave-like strain distribution. Accordingly, the otherwise damage-prone stress concentrations can be relieved by the well-tuned atomic-scale strain waves. This approach can also boost planar slip, further promoting the strain hardening ability in the loading stages. The present study thus suggests a promising path toward the development of strong and ductile lightweight steels for advanced structural engineering applications.

---

## Results

The present lightweight steel in homogenized condition is characterized by a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC-γ) austenitic structure, showing homogeneous elemental distribution at the micro-scale without any grain boundary (GB) precipitates (Supplementary Figure 2). The stacking fault energy (SFE) of the steel is relatively high, i.e., ~82 mJ/m2 according to the weak-beam dark-field (DF) STEM characterization (Supplementary Figure 3) and ~78 mJ/m2 calculated by the subregular solution model6,20 (see Supplementary Information). The atomic-scale strain wave in the material was tuned via adjusting the time periods of annealing after cold-rolling. The samples annealed at 900 oC for short time (3 min) and that for longer time (30 min) are denoted as SA and LA, respectively. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Supplementary Figure 4) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) phase maps (Fig. 1a, b) reveal the FCC structure in both LA and SA bulk steels. As shown in Fig. 1a-b, abundant annealing twin boundaries (TBs) are present in both steels. The average grain sizes excluding annealing TBs in steels LA and SA are 15.0 ± 9.7 μm and 7.5 ± 5.4 μm, respectively, according to EBSD analysis from multiple areas in each sample. The bright-field (BF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images (Supplementary Figure 5a, c) and corresponding energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mappings (Supplementary Figure 5b, d) suggest that the steels LA and SA show homogeneous elemental distribution at the micro- and nano-scales. In the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns (inserts in Fig. 1c, d) taken along the zone axis of [001] , the inherently faint γ diffraction spots from specific {100} superlattice diffraction signal of κ'-carbide are visible in both steels LA and SA. More specifically, dark-field (DF) imaging was used to visualize the κ'-carbide domains and the results are shown in Fig. 1c, d, which indicates that the average sizes of κ'-carbide are 0.4 nm and 0.5 nm with average area fractions of 8.5% and 16.5% in steels LA and SA, respectively. The abnormal decreases of fraction and size of the sub-nanoscale κ'-carbides with increasing annealing time from 3 min to 30 min is related to the formation kinetics of κ'-carbide. Specifically, the high atomic mobility promoted by crystalline defects induced in the prior deformation strongly facilitates the formation kinetics of sub-nanoscale κ'-carbides during annealing at the first few minutes, leading to the deviation of associated crystal lattice from thermodynamic equilibrium. However, upon further increasing annealing time, the prolonged exposure of the fully recrystallized microstructure at 900 oC can lead to the partial dissolution of the previously formed sub-nanoscale κ'-carbide, rendering the crystal lattice closer to the thermodynamic equilibrium state.

Atomic-resolution high-angle angular dark field (HAADF) STEM technique was performed in the exploration of the κ'-carbide domains in steels LA and SA. The atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images overlapped with the inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) maps in Fig. 1e, f outline the distribution of κ'-carbide domains in the FCC lattices of the two steels, whereas the contrasts of the different atomic columns indicates that the elements are nonuniformly distributed at the atomic-scale. The atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM image of steel LA acquired along [011] γ zone axis in Supplementary Figure 6a and the EDS analysis result in Supplementary Figure 6b, c suggest that Al tends to be enriched in specific atomic columns. The atomic-scale distributions of Fe and Mn are also inhomogeneous, but are more uniform compared to that of Al. Specifically, Fe-rich columns are Mn-depleted, and the two types of atomic columns are adjacent to each other. This may arise from the zero mixing enthalpy between Fe and Mn, and thus they neither attract nor repel each other21,22. The negative mixing enthalpies of Fe-Al (-11 KJ/mol) and Mn-Al (-19 KJ/mol)23 provide the thermodynamic driving force for the formation of κ'-carbide. In the κ'-carbide domains, the average atomic fractions of Fe, Mn and Al for atomic columns on the (11̅1) plane show wave-like fluctuations with wavelength doubling the spacing of the crystal plane (Supplementary Figure 6d).

Atom probe tomography (APT) was also performed to analyze chemical features of the κ'-carbides. The 3D reconstruction maps of typical cubes in Supplementary Figure 7e, f show the clustering behavior in steels LA and SA, respectively. The calculated radial distribution functions (RDFs) of Fe and Mn around Al atoms (Supplementary Figure 7g) show bulk-normalized Al-(Fe/Mn) concentration ratios exceeding unity at the subnanoscale. Notably, these ratios are higher in steel SA than that in steel LA, indicating that more Al-(Fe/Mn) bonds contribute to the formation of κ'-carbide domains in steel SA. This is consistent with the statistical results for the fractions of κ'-carbides from the DF-TEM images in Fig. 1c, d. The average Al concentration within the κ'-carbides is ~18.1 at. % and ~22.3 at. % for steels LA and SA, respectively. Since the atomic radius of Al (0.143 nm) is remarkably larger than Fe/Mn (0.124 nm), significant lattice expansion and contraction can occur at the Al-rich κ'-carbide domains and Al-depleted FCC-γ matrix, respectively, which can further induce atomic-scale strain fluctuations in the steels.

The atomic-scale strain fluctuation was further explored by the geometric phase analysis (GPA) method25,26 based on HAADF-STEM images, e.g., shown in Fig. 1g, h. The ε strain maps xx show the atomic-scale tension-compression strain distributions in steels LA and SA with statistical average strain values (total pixels) of 0.26% nm-2 and 1.06% nm-2, respectively (Fig. 1g, h). This indicates that steel LA undergoes greater lattice expansion than steel SA. Further, the results suggest that the atomic-scale strain waves are primarily derived from the lattice expansion and contraction at the sub-nano-sized Al-rich κ'-carbide domains and Al-depleted FCC-γ matrix, respectively, resulting in a fluctuating tension-compression strain distribution at atomic scale. Fig. 1i shows the line profiles of atomic-scale strains along the [200] γ direction, revealing the wave-like distribution with crests and valleys. The average wavelength of atomic-scale strains along the [200] γ direction in steel SA (0.84 ± 0.27 nm) is smaller than that in steel LA (0.98 ± 0.38 nm), while the average amplitude in steel SA (1.71 ± 0.70%) is higher than that in steel LA (0.82 ± 0.32%). The ε strain maps in Supplementary Figure 8 also shows the higher strain amplitude and smaller wavelength of the atomic-scale strains in steel SA than those in steel LA. This can be attributed to the higher Al concentration and larger fraction of κ'-carbides in steel SA, as discussed above.

Further, the original steels LA and SA were aged at 600 oC for 40 min to trigger the formation of nanosized L1 -(Fe, Mn) AlC (x<1) κ-carbide, and the resultant materials are denoted by LA-A and SA-A, respectively. XRD patterns (Supplementary Figure 4) and EBSD phase maps (Supplementary Figure 9a, e) confirm the FCC structure in both LA-A and SA-A bulk steels. The average grain sizes excluding annealing TBs in steels LA-A and SA-A are equal to steels LA and SA, respectively, according to EBSD analysis from multiple areas in each sample. This confirms that the aging treatment did not change the grain sizes in the steels. The EDS mappings (Supplementary Figure 9d, h) for the areas captured by BF-STEM images (Supplementary Figure 9c, g) suggest homogeneous elemental distribution at the micro-scale in both steels. However, in the SAED patterns in Fig. 2a, b taken along the zone axis of [001] γ, the {100} superlattice diffraction spots of κ'- and κ-carbides with ordered structures are distinctly visible in both steels LA and SA. This is consistent to the previous finding that the κ'-carbide can serve as a precursor for the formation of κ-carbide by further ordering of C into the body-centered octahedral interstitial positions via spinodal decomposition 6,7. The DF images stemming from the diffraction spot of (110) κ'/κ in Fig. 2c, d light up the κ- and κ'-carbide domains. The average sizes of κ-carbide in steels LA-A and SA-A are 6.1 ± 1.7 nm and 6.0 ± 1.2 nm, respectively. The HAADF-STEM images in Fig. 2e and f reveal the atomic-scale structures of κ-carbides in steels LA-A and SA-A, respectively. The ε xx strain maps in Fig. 2g, h by GPA method using the vectors of (200) γ and (020) γ also show the wave-like tension-compression strain fluctuations in atomic scale. The statistical strain values (total pixels) are 16.87% nm-2 and 6.5% nm-2 in steels LA-A and SA-A, respectively. Fig. 2i shows the line profiles of atomic-scale strains along the [020] γ direction. The matrixes containing sub-nano-sized κ'-carbide domains show atomic-scale strain waves with the average amplitude of 1.84 ± 0.89% and 1.01 ± 0.48% in steels SA-A and LA-A, respectively, similar to those in the as-annealed steels without aging (SA and LA). Moreover, the interiors of aging-induced nano-sized κ-carbide phase regions in steels SA-A and LA-A also exhibit wave-like periodic fluctuations with the average amplitude of 1.59 ± 0.42% and 1.16 ± 0.58%, respectively. For the steel LA-A, the atomic-scale strain waves in the κ-carbide phase are almost tension with average value of wave peaks and troughs to be about 1.58%, which is higher than that in the matrix (~0.06%), suggesting that the atomic-scale strain distributions in the κ-carbide and matrix are distinctly different. However, in the steel SA-A, the atomic-scale strain distributions in the κ-carbide and matrix are fairly similar as indicated by the small differences in average amplitudes (1.59% and 1.84%, respectively) and average strain values (0.09% and -0.24%, respectively).

Fig. 3a shows the tensile engineering stress-strain curves of the steels at room temperature. The steel SA characterized by atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength exhibits a yield strength value (𝜎 y) of 687 ± 13 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (𝜎 u) of 1154 ± 4 MPa and a total elongation (𝜀 f) of 67.8% ± 4.0%, which are significantly higher than those values of steel LA (610 ± 10 MPa, 1035 ± 9 MPa and 37.8% ± 2.3%, respectively) with atomic-scale strain waves of lower amplitude and larger wavelength. The enhancements in strength and ductility achieved by tuning atomic-scale strain waves can also be observed when comparing the steels SA-A and LA-A with κ-carbide precipitation strengthening effect. More specific, the steel SA-A has a yield strength (𝜎 y) of 1073 ± 10 MPa and an ultimate tensile strength (𝜎 u) of 1325 ± 8 MPa at a total elongation (𝜀 f) of 50.4% ± 3.2%, which are superior than those of steel LA-A (1051 ± 8 MPa, 1242 ± 13 MPa and 20.1% ± 1.3%, respectively). The steels SA and SA-A exhibit not only enhanced strength and ductility but also superior work-hardening abilities compared to steels LA and LA-A, respectively (Fig. 3b). This is correlated with the modulated dislocation behaviors via tuning atomic-scale strain waves, as specifically discussed next. The above results suggest that the current strategy of tuning atomic-scale strain waves can allow for overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off that are presented in previous steels. Moreover, this strategy can be combined with the coherent nanoprecipitation approach to jointly enhance the strength-ductility combination, as can be confirmed by comparing the tensile curves of the present aged steels containing nano-sized κ-carbides (SA-A, LA-A) and that of the as-annealed variants free of nano-sized κ-carbides (SA, LA).

To avoid sample size effect, the uniform elongation values were used in the comparison of strength-ductility combinations shown in Fig. 3c (see details in Supplementary Table 3). Evidently, the strength-ductility combinations of the present lightweight steels SA and SA-A surpass that of previous lightweight steels, including those with κ-carbide precipitation strengthening 11,12,17,27,28, κ-carbide plus B2 particles strengthening 1,9,13,15,29, and duplex structure composed of FCC-γ and BCC-α phases with κ-carbide precipitation strengthening 18,19,30,31. Further, the products of specific ultimate tensile strength (SUTS) and uniform elongation (UE) of the steels SA and SA-A reach 8.5 and 7.4 GPa·g-1·cm3·%, respectively, which are unprecedentedly high compared to those obtained in previous studies, as shown in Fig. 3d. We also converted the total elongation values from references and our work into those corresponding to identical standard specimen dimensions by the Barba’s law, and accordingly the converted total elongation (CTE) is used in the additional comparison (see the calculation details in Supplementary Information) 32-34. As presented in Supplementary Figure 11, the products of SUTS and CTE of the present lightweight steels SA and SA-A surpass that of the previous lightweight steels.

The atomic-scale strain waves can also modulate the lattice constants of the present lightweight steels (Supplementary Table 2) and thus affect the elastic moduli. As displayed in Supplementary Table 4, the elastic moduli of steels SA and SA-A are higher than those of steels LA and LA-A, respectively. Further, shear modulus associated with the elastic modulus is of significance for determining the Peierls-Nabarro (P-N) stress that required to make a dislocation glide in a crystal without the assistance of thermal activation. Accordingly, the yield strength values for steels SA and LA ascribed from the significant lattice friction are estimated to be ~590 MPa and ~581 MPa, respectively (see the calculation details in Supplementary Information). Grain boundary strengthening also act as an effective mechanism that contribute to the yield strength of the steels, and the corresponding values for steels SA (average grain size of ~7.5 μm) and LA (average grain size of ~15.0 μm) are ~208 MPa and ~147 MPa, respectively (see Supplementary Information). In addition, the κ-carbide can provide significant precipitation strengthening as can be demonstrated by the observation that the yield strength values of steels LA-A and SA-A are higher than steels LA and SA, respectively. Further calculations suggest that the precipitation strengthening contributions from the κ-carbide for steels LA-A and SA-A are ~468 MPa and ~460 MPa, respectively (see Supplementary Information).

To elucidate the underlying deformation mechanisms responsible for the enhanced mechanical properties of the present steels, the deformed microstructures in the tensile-tested samples were characterized and compared at the identical deformation stages with various local strain levels at micro-, nano- and atomic scales. At the medium uniform deformation stages of steels LA and LA-A (i.e., local strains of ~20% and ~10%, respectively), the microstructures are characterized by a series of discrete planar slip bands along {111} γ planes with statistical average spacing of 411.6 ± 168.6 nm and 94.2 ± 86.3 nm, respectively, as shown in Fig. 4a and b. The intense dislocations that progressively tangled into high-density dislocation walls (HDDWs) along intersecting {111} γ slip planes are also observed. With increasing local strain to ~45% for steel LA at the late uniform deformation stage, the deformation microstructures are characterized by the progressive refinement of slip bands with a statistical average spacing reduction to 54.8 ± 35.8 nm (Fig. 4c). For steel LA-A, when local strain increases to ~15% (late uniform deformation stage), it maintains comparable slip band spacing of 93.4 ± 79.2 nm relative to prior strain levels (Fig. 4d). During the necking stages, upon further increasing local strain to ~70% and ~30% for steels LA and LA-A, the average spacings of slip bands are 54.4 ± 20.1 nm and 91.6 ± 58.3 nm, respectively (Supplementary Figure 12 and 13), suggesting that further slip band refinement in both steels is insignificant. Also, the distribution of slip bands is relatively heterogeneous, particularly in steel LA-A (Supplementary Figures 12 and 13).

The deformation microstructures of steels SA and SA-A are shown in Fig. 4e-h. At local strains of ~15% and ~10% (early uniform deformation stages) for steels SA and SA-A, respectively, the paired dislocations are regularly arranged within the matrix (Fig. 4e, f). The planar slip bands are also observed along {111} γ planes in the steel SA as displayed in Fig. 4e, with a statistical average spacing of 121.7 ± 49.7 nm. The increase of local strains to ~50% and ~30% at late uniform deformation stages for steels SA and SA-A, respectively, leads to the significant multiplication of planar slip bands and the increase in the number density of dislocations within individual bands, as displayed in Fig. 4g, h. At these strain levels, the statistical average spacings of slip bands in steels SA and SA-A are 39.3 ± 14.0 nm and 76.8 ± 47.5 nm, respectively. The nanoscale well-organized hexagonal dislocation networks on {111} γ planes are observed in both steels SA and SA-A. Further increasing local strains to ~75% and ~50% for steels SA and SA-A during necking stages leads to the reducing of slip band spacings to 34.3 ± 14.1 nm and 48.8 ± 30.7 nm, respectively (Supplementary Figures 12 and 13).

According to the above results, the morphologies of dislocations in plastically deformed steels SA and SA-A at early and medium uniform deformation stages are distinctly different. This is clearly illustrated by the amplified LAADF-STEM images in Supplementary Figure 14 which shows paired dislocations in steel SA and long dislocation lines in steel LA. This suggests that the atomic-scale strain waves in the steels significantly affect the slip of dislocations and thus their configuration. When the slip of leading dislocation is barriered by the strain wave peaks or troughs, the succeeding dislocation is likely to pile up and aggregate around the nearby region, which facilitates the formation of paired dislocations35. Also, in front of a dislocation line, the strain waves can induce the fluctuations of driving force levels. Thus, the dislocations slip by nanoscale segments that cut through the peaks or troughs of the strain waves. This results in a variant of stick-slip, and the moving dislocation lines become wavy as each segment responds differently. The conversion of an initially straight dislocation line into a wavy configuration also shortens the length to minimize the total energy of the dislocations. This rationalizes the shorter paired-dislocations in steel SA compared with the longer and smoother dislocation lines in steel LA (Supplementary Figure 14). The mechanisms for the formation of short and wavy paired dislocations can also be activated in steel SA-A. Thus, the atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength lead to the local pinning effect that makes overall dislocation movement sluggish, improving the strength levels of steels SA and SA-A.

In the present study, typical planar slip bands are observed in the deformed microstructures of the steels at various local strain levels, which are also commonly found in previous lightweight steels12,36,37. The inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) images in Fig. 4i, j shows the planar slip planes marked by red arrows and the edge dislocations with the Burgers vector of 𝑎/2 [01̅1] for steels LA and SA (with local strains of ~20% and ~15%, respectively). The formation of slip bands by dislocation planar slip is closely related to the stacking fault energy (SFE). The generalized SFE of the present lightweight steel estimated by thermodynamic calculation is ~78 mJ/m2 and the experimentally measured value is ~82 mJ/m2 (see Supplementary Information), which are comparably high. This SFE level would facilitate the planar slip in the steel during plastic deformation38. Notably, the local SFE can be variable from one site to another in the present lightweight steels due to the chemical fluctuation caused by the κ'-carbide. More specific, high Al concentration zones at κ'-carbide domains can be incorporated to push the magnitude of SFE up, while Fe/Mn-rich zones are particularly effective in reducing the local SFE39,40. The lower local SFE can widen the dissociate distance of two Shockley partial dislocations, which promotes the planar slip of dislocations on the initial slip plane. Thus, the atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength in steels SA and SA-A can bring in drastic fluctuations of local SFE and promote the planar slip of dislocations during plastic deformation. The planar slip of shorter paired dislocations in steels SA and SA-A bring finer slip bands than that in steels LA and LA-A (Supplementary Figure 13). Then the formation and refinement of planar slip bands during plastic deformation can provide significant dynamic Hall-Petch effect for enhancing strain-hardening ability over the deformation process, which significantly contributes to the high ductility at high strength levels41.

During plastic deformation, when the movement of dislocations is hindered on its primary slip plane, the increasing strain can promote a propensity for cross-slip of dislocations to accommodate plastic flow. The possibility of dislocation cross-slip strongly depends on the SFE. The relatively high SFE of the present steels can facilitate dislocation cross-slip by narrowing the dissociation width of perfect dislocations. This also helps to store dislocations and promotes their reactions in the steels. In the steels LA and LA-A, the cross-slip of long dislocation lines can facilitate the formation of HDDWs during plastic deformation, which can induce stress localization and is certainly adverse to the ductility42. Notably, the short paired dislocations in steels SA and SA-A can cross-slip and lead to the formation of dense hexagonal dislocation networks43. This corresponds to shorter dislocation lines and hence lower energy, which can significantly improve the tolerance for dislocation accumulation in the steels during plastic deformation. With the increased dislocation storage capacity, the dynamic formation of hexagonal dislocation networks significantly enhance the strain hardening ability and strength-ductility synergy.

In summary, we have developed unprecedentedly strong and ductile lightweight steel by inducing significant atomic-scale alternating tension-compression strain waves, which are formed by lattice expansion in Al-rich short-range ordered κ'-carbide domains and contraction in Fe/Mn-rich FCC-γ matrix. Upon mechanical loading, these atomic-scale strain waves with high amplitude and small wavelength significantly increase the lattice friction, contributing to the high yield strength. During plastic deformation, the atomic-scale strain waves convert the straight dislocation lines into wavy and paired. The increase of engineering strains can force the paired dislocations tangle into dense hexagonal dislocation networks via cross-slip, which significantly enhances the defect-storage capacity of the steel. The atomic-scale strain waves can also promote the dynamic microstructure refinement with the reduction in the average spacing of planar slip bands during plastic deformation. These mechanisms jointly suppress localized stress concentrations and promote strain hardening ability, rendering the steels ultra-strong and ductile. The demonstrated strategy of tuning atomic-scale strain waves is thus promising for guiding the development of ultra-strong and ductile lightweight materials for advanced structural engineering applications.

## Methods

Thermodynamic calculations
The thermodynamic calculations by Factsage software 8.3 with the FSstel database were carried out to design the Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight steel. The phase diagrams illustrating the phase evolution with respect to the variations of C, Al and Mn contents and temperature are given in Supplementary Figure 1a-c, respectively. The C content of 5 at.% was selected to achieve a single FCC-γ phase above ~900 °C and κ-carbide precipitation below ~650 °C. To avoid the presence of BCC-α ferrite, the Al content of 15 at.% was chosen for the design. Additionally, a relatively high Mn content of 30 at.% was selected due to its role in stabilizing austenitic matrix and reducing the precipitation temperature of κ-carbide. As illustrated in Supplementary Figure 1d, the predicted phase configurations in the designed Fe Mn Al C lightweight steel indicate the high potential to achieve a microstructure consisting of austenite matrix and κ-carbide precipitates.

Material processing
A 5 kg Fe Mn Al C lightweight steel ingot, prepared using a commercial vacuum-induction furnace by melting pure Fe, Mn, Al and graphite (purity >99.9 wt.%), was ordered outside. The exact chemical compositions of the lightweight steel measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) and carbon-sulfur analyzer (CS744) are listed in Supplementary Table 1. A piece of lightweight steel with a thickness of 10 mm was cut from the ingot followed by hot rolling at 900 oC with a thickness reduction of 50%. Then the plate was homogenized at 1200 oC for 2 h followed by water quenching. Cold-rolling was conducted with a thickness reduction of 70%. Recrystallization annealing processes with short time (3 min) and longer time (30 min) were conducted at 900 oC followed by water quenching, and the annealed steel samples are denoted as LA and SA, respectively. Precipitation aging was performed at 600 oC for 40 min based on steels LA and SA, and the aged steel samples are denoted as LA-A and SA-A, respectively. During homogenization, annealing and aging, the lightweight steel samples were hermetically sealed in vacuum quartz tubes to avoid oxidation. The heat treatments were carried out in a box furnace and ended with water quenching in a water bath.

Mechanical characterization
Rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and a gauge width of 2.5 mm were machined inhouse by electrical discharge machining (DK 7720, China) according to the standard of ASTM E8 (different specimen sizes are allowed) 44. Room temperature uniaxial tensile tests were conducted by a Sansi 10 kN machine with an engineering strain rate of 1×10-3 s-1. The digital image correlation (DIC) method using the Aramis system (GOM GmbH) was used to precisely determine local strain evolution during tensile testing.

The product of specific ultimate tensile strength (SUTS) and tensile elongation (TE) was calculated as (UTS×TE)/𝜌, where 𝜌 is the mass density. The mass density of the present steel are estimated based on the regression formula45:
1/𝜌 = ∑ 𝐶𝑖/𝜌𝑖 (1)
where 𝜌𝑖 is the mass density of element i and 𝐶𝑖 is the mass fraction of element i.

The elastic modulus and nanohardness values were determined by nanoindentation at room temperature using a KLA G200X indentation tester with a Berkovich tip. During nanoindentation test, 16 indents were arranged in a square with the spacing between adjacent indents of 5 μm to avoid the overlap of plastic zones.

Microstructural characterization
The phase constituents of the steel samples were measured by X-ray diffraction (D/max-B 2550, Rigaku, Japan) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis with Hough transform was carried out using a Tescan Clara scanning electron microscope (SEM) with EDAX OIM data collection software at a voltage of 20.0 keV and 7.0 nA with a working distance of 15.0 mm and a step size of 100 nm. Back-scattered electron (BSE) imaging and electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) were performed at a voltage of 30.0 keV and 3.0 nA with a working distance of 10.0 mm. Energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) analysis based on the SEM was carried out with a working distance of 15.0 mm. The average grain sizes of the steels were determined based on EBSD measurements using TSL OIM 8.0 analysis software, with all data points above a threshold CI (Confidence Index) value of 0.1. The samples for SEM observations were prepared by grinding using silicon carbide paper from 400 to 5000 granulation and polishing using 3 μm diamond suspension and 20 nm silica dioxide suspension.

For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis, a ThermoFisher Talos F200X instrument was operated at a voltage of 200 kV. The probe convergence angle was 10.6 mrad for STEM imaging. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF), low-angle annular dark-field (LAADF) and bright field (BF) STEM images were obtained at collecting angles of 50-200 mrad, 30-50 mrad, and 0-30 mrad, respectively. The ThermoFisher Spectra 300 instrument was also used for atomic-resolution STEM observation operated at a voltage of 300 kV. The probe convergence angle and collecting angle for the atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images were 25.0 mrad and 50-200 mrad, respectively. To prepare samples for S/TEM analysis, disc specimens with a diameter of 3 mm were cut from the gauge region of tensile-tested samples at various local strain levels and non-deformation samples and ground to a thickness of ~50 μm followed by electron polishing using a twin-jet electron-polisher at a temperature of -30 °C. The electrolyte used for the electron polishing was a solution of 90% methanol and 10% perchloric acid. The atomic-scale strain maps were obtained by the geometric phase analysis (GPA) method based on the atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images using the strain++ 1.7.1 software. To ensure high reliability of the strain results, HAADF-STEM imaging was performed with drift correction by the piezo stage controller. The image was reconstructed after filtering out high-frequency noise to improve the signal‐to‐noise ratio, thereby enhancing the precision and accuracy of atomic-scale strain measurements 24.

For atom probe tomography (APT) analysis, the tips were prepared inhouse by a two-stage electro-polishing method. In the first stage, the samples with dimensions of 0.5×0.5×10 mm were polished using a 25 vol% perchloric/acetic acid solution at 15 V under the D.C. condition to prepare a rough needle. Then the needle samples were polished to a suitable sharpness using 2 vol% perchloric acid in 2-butoxyethanol solution at 5 V under the D.C. condition. APT analysis was carried out using CAMECA LEAP 5000 XR in voltage-pulsing mode with a repetition rate of 200 kHz and a pulse fraction of 15% at 50 K.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer for the valuable comments. We have carefully
confirmed the microstructures of the steel SA annealed at 900 oC for 3 min with the
low-magnification BSE image (field view of 733 × 550 μm) prior to the EBSD analysis,
which shows the fully recrystallized grains. We have added the overview BSE image
of the steels LA (annealing at 900 oC for 30 min) and SA (annealing at 900 oC for 3 min)
in the Supplementary materials. It is then confirmed that our experimental results of the
fully recrystallized microstructure of the steel SA can be reproduced.
The short-time annealing process at 900 oC for 3 min was used for constructing
the special atomic-scale strain waves of high amplitude and small wavelength in the
lightweight steel. It is worth noting that such annealing process was performed on the
cold-rolled plate with a thickness of 1.5 mm. The corresponding microstructures in Fig.
S5 demonstrate that this short duration is sufficient to uniformly treat the sample,
causing recovery of dislocations and building recrystallized grains with annealing twins.
When considering hot-rolled or cold-rolled sheets with relatively small thickness in
practical application (e.g., thickness of 1.5 mm in this study), this short-time annealing
process can be adopted, as it enables rapid and uniform temperature distribution along
the thickness direction. However, for practical applications involving parts with large
thickness, this short-time duration annealing process is likely to be not suitable as
concerned by the reviewer. In the present study, the high amplitude and small
wavelength atomic-scale strain waves can be triggered by the short-time annealing
process, which is of significance to modulate the dislocations behavior. The main
findings can provide insights for designing stronger and more ductile materials with
such atomic-scale structures by various annealing process with different temperatures
and durations. Namely, the specific annealing temperature and duration can be finely
tuned for material parts with different dimensions to obtain the similar structures.
The short-time annealing process has been applied in various alloys, with the aim
of constructing different micro- or nano-structures to meet various requirements of
mechanical properties. For example, in Cu alloys, a balance of strength-ductility
synergy and residual stress can be modulated by annealing at 200 oC for 1 min [Journal
of alloys and compounds, 2023, 941: 168705]. The fine structure within β phase in Ti-
6Al-4V alloy, which is highly sensitive to the solution heat treatment temperature, can
be optimized by annealing at 915 °C/120 s and 570 °C/180 s, significantly enhancing
the strength [Materials Science and Engineering: A, 2025, 926: 147787]. The short-
time annealing process, akin to ultra-fast heating technique in steel industry, has been
proposed to meet the requirements for energy and production efficiency with high-
quality. The short time exposure at a certain temperature significantly increases strength
without sacrificing a substantial amount of ductility, which worked by effectively refine
the grain size, induce the heterogeneous structure, stabilize the austenite and inhibit the
formation of brittle phase [Materials & Design, 2024, 238: 112658]. It has also been
reported that the ultra-fast heating at 730 oC for 100 s leads to the formation of retained
austenite grains, inheriting the chemical composition of strain-induced martensite with
a high density of dislocations in middle-Mn steel, which significant increases yield
strength by 270 MPa and the product of strength and elongation up to 55 GPa% due to
the enormous work hardening capacity [Journal of Materials Science & Technology,
2022, 97: 54-68].
In summary, the microstructures of steel SA are uniform with fully recrystallized
grains. Such a short-time annealing process can be applied to the hot-rolled or cold-
rolled sheets with relatively small thickness (e.g., thickness of 1.5 mm in this study).
Similar short-time annealing process has been widely applied for various materials with
the aim of tuning microstructures to enhance the mechanical properties.
